title: Lists and Keys
summary: Rendering lists in React means mapping an array of data to an array of JSX elements using .map(). Each element in the list must have a unique key prop so React can efficiently track which items changed, were added, or removed. Keys should be stable identifiers (like database IDs), not array indices — using indices causes bugs when the list is reordered or filtered.
keyPoints: Use .map() to transform an array of data into an array of JSX elements
Every element in a list needs a unique key prop: <li key={item.id}>
Keys help React identify which items changed, were added, or removed
Use stable, unique IDs as keys — not array indices
Array index as key causes issues with reordering, filtering, and component state
Keys must be unique among siblings, not globally
The key prop is not passed to the component — it is used by React internally

exercises.prompt:
Which correctly renders a list of movie titles?

const movies = [{ id: 1, title: 'Inception' }, { id: 2, title: 'Dune' }]
exercises.explanation: .map() returns a new array of JSX elements that React can render. forEach returns undefined and cannot be used in JSX. Each element needs a unique key.

exercises.prompt: Why do list items need a key prop?
options: So React can efficiently track and update individual items
Keys are optional — React works fine without them
exercises.answer: So React can efficiently track and update individual items
exercises.explanation: Keys let React match elements across renders. Without keys, React re-renders the entire list on any change. With keys, it only updates the items that actually changed.

exercises.prompt:
Why is using array index as a key problematic?

movies.map((m, index) => <MovieCard key={index} ... />)
options: Indices change when items are reordered, added, or removed — causing incorrect component reuse
React does not accept numbers as keys
It only fails in production mode
exercises.answer: Indices change when items are reordered, added, or removed — causing incorrect component reuse
exercises.explanation: If you remove the first item, the second item gets key=0 (which was the first item's key). React thinks it is the same component and reuses its state, causing bugs.

exercises.prompt: What happens if you forget the key prop on list items?
options: React shows a console warning and performance may degrade
The list renders in reverse order
exercises.answer: React shows a console warning and performance may degrade
exercises.explanation: React still renders the list but warns in the console. Without keys, React cannot optimize updates and may re-render more elements than necessary.

exercises.prompt: Which is a valid key for a list of movies fetched from an API?
exercises.explanation: Database IDs are ideal keys — they are stable and unique. Math.random() creates a new key every render, destroying and recreating all components. Index keys cause reorder bugs.

exercises.prompt:
Is the key prop accessible inside the child component?

<MovieCard key={movie.id} title={movie.title} />
options: No — key is consumed by React and not passed as a prop
Yes — but only in class components
exercises.answer: No — key is consumed by React and not passed as a prop
exercises.explanation: React uses key internally for reconciliation. If you need the id inside the component, pass it as a separate prop: <MovieCard key={movie.id} id={movie.id} />.

exercises.prompt:
Complete the code to render a <ul> with an <li> for each fruit:

const fruits = [{ id: 'a', name: 'Apple' }, { id: 'b', name: 'Banana' }]
exercises.explanation: Use .map() to transform each fruit object into an <li> element with a unique key from the id property.
